lesson.title: Putting It All Together: The Anatomy of a Dataset
lesson.summary: This section shows how variables and observations combine into a dataset, typically arranged as a rectangular table, and works through summarizing a small classroom dataset.
lesson.body:
A dataset is what you get when many observations of the same set of variables are collected and organized together into a single structured whole. If a variable is a column and an observation is a row, then a dataset is the entire table: every row and every column together. Datasets are almost always arranged this way, as a rectangle, because a rectangular layout guarantees that every individual has a recorded value for every variable, or an explicit marker that the value is missing, which keeps the information organized and comparable.

Consider the full classroom dataset built from the pieces introduced in the last two sections. The teacher tracked 2 variables, quiz score and height, across 8 students. Laid out as a table, the dataset has 8 rows, one per student observation, and 2 columns, one per variable, for a total of 16 individual recorded values. The quiz scores, reading down that column, are 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 5, 8, 10. The heights, reading down the other column, are 61, 64, 58, 66, 63, 59, 65, 60. Reading across any single row gives you one complete observation: a specific student's quiz score paired with that same student's height.

One of the biggest advantages of organizing data this way is that it allows you to compute summaries that describe the whole group rather than any one individual. Take the height column as a worked example. Adding the 8 heights gives 61 + 64 + 58 + 66 + 63 + 59 + 65 + 60. Working through that sum step by step: 61 plus 64 is 125, plus 58 is 183, plus 66 is 249, plus 63 is 312, plus 59 is 371, plus 65 is 436, plus 60 is 496. Dividing that total, 496, by the number of students, 8, gives an average height of 62.0 inches. That single number, 62.0, summarizes an entire column of the dataset, but it only means something because the dataset was organized consistently, with every height correctly matched to a real student.

Datasets are not limited to two variables or eight rows. Real statistical datasets can have thousands of rows and dozens of columns, tracking anything from hospital patient records to weather station readings to daily stock prices. The organizing logic never changes, though: rows are observations, columns are variables, and every individual value sits at the intersection of exactly one row and one column. Learning to read a dataset this way, rather than as an undifferentiated block of numbers, is one of the most practically useful skills in this entire course.

Later sections will look more closely at the columns of a dataset and ask what kind of variable each one is. Some columns, like eye color or favorite subject, sort students into named categories. Other columns, like quiz score or height, record numbers that can be added, averaged, and compared using arithmetic. That distinction, between categorical and quantitative variables, determines almost every choice you make about how to summarize and visualize a dataset.
